name: Victor Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead ambulance-dispatch software at a tech company, where I am among the strongest developers. I use AI every day to draft address tests, but compare results with the dispatch log. Salma works at a tree nursery, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with five months of expenses saved and some other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the ambulance-dispatch team that a small AI shortcut can find a duplicate address, but a caller still needs the right vehicle sent. I use AI every day to draft code tests and check them against the dispatch log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this system at a tech company; I am one of the stronger developers in the team. Salma works at a tree nursery, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing one wrong-address report with the dispatcher each Friday. We would save 160 monthly while both wages hold and repair our old garden steps rather than replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our jobs and bills here. An ambulance sent to the wrong street is not made less late by a tidy log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What address went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caller gave a block number that matched two streets. I checked the recorded call time against the map and had the dispatcher confirm the right entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it for awkward address test cases. I still run the case and compare the response with the dispatcher’s actual rule before release.

I use **AI daily** for draft tests, then verify the log.
think: I have **five months saved** on typical lead pay.
I see **rent covered** while both current wages continue.
do: **Review wrong addresses** with dispatchers each Friday.
**Save 160 monthly** while both wages hold; repair garden steps before replacing them.

fieldNote: His **lead skill** concerns dispatch reliability, not claiming to be a paramedic.
The **five-month reserve** supports current security despite uncertainty about future dispatch work and without relying on grown children.

Save 160 monthly while both household wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, answering customers, checking and coding could reduce dispatch-software staff. We need a dispatcher’s sign-off before any automated priority change reaches a live call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid lead hours could shrink even if the system still needs scrutiny. Five months saved gives us time, but Salma’s nursery wage alone would not cover our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to pilot a new AI call-priority checker on synthetic dispatch calls, with a trained dispatcher reviewing every flagged case. If approved, I’d test one mistaken high-priority call weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local emergency-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and eager to test the tool. A coloured priority flag is not a patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who approves a live change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatcher lead must review the test, and my manager must approve deployment. I would not put a new priority rule on live calls from an AI suggestion alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use real calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the service gives explicit permission and strips identifying details. For the initial pilot I would use made-up calls on paid time.

say: I want **dispatcher sign-off** before AI call priorities reach live ambulance crews.
I want **synthetic calls** used for paid testing before any real patient is affected.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** to automated triage.
I cannot use **Salma’s nursery wage** alone for bills.
do: **Pilot AI priority checker** weekly only with approved paid time, synthetic calls and trained dispatcher review.
**Search paid emergency software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: A coloured priority flag is not a patient.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** differs from everyday drafted tests and needs paid approval plus dispatch review.
The **local job search** starts only if his lead hours fall and a paid vacancy covers bills.

steps.text: Pilot AI priority checker weekly only with approved paid time, synthetic calls and trained dispatcher review
Search paid local emergency-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write dispatch code and answer emergency calls cheaper than our team. Robots driving ambulances and working in nurseries may follow around 2031, after the screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer role could end even if I can explain its hardest failures. Five months saved would buy search time, but Salma’s nursery wage alone would not replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d defer our planned kitchen refit and request written notice of lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local emergency-operations vacancies only if they exist, I meet current requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office which temporary support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the main wage. An emergency log cannot answer our landlord when rent is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would operations jobs also face AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I would not call one a safe refuge. I would take only an actual paid opening that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check local emergency services and software firms. Salma’s nursery work and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach dispatch code first.
I expect **ambulance robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead wage** could end quickly.
I know **five months saved** is a finite search buffer.
do: **Defer kitchen refit** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for emergency operations** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: An emergency log cannot answer our landlord when rent is due.
fieldNote: His **operations route** is a conditional paid vacancy, not a protected job.
He checks **actual public eligibility** without counting unconfirmed support as a replacement for his lead wage.

steps.text: Defer planned kitchen refit and request written lead-cut notice now
Apply for qualified paid local emergency-operations vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives services time to identify which emergency calls still need a trained human decision. Robots driving ambulances may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn call handling while earning my developer wage, but building the code does not qualify me to answer a caller in distress. I would need paid supervised practice and a real service willing to train me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the ambulance service and my employer for a paid monthly practice shift using simulated emergency calls with a qualified dispatcher. If both approve and the service funds supervision, I’d complete the call-handling lessons; we would save 145 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local dispatcher openings only if certified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code role but willing to learn a different responsibility. A calm voice on a test call has to survive a real frightened caller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the location, repeat it back and follow the service’s priority script. The dispatcher would correct my mistakes before any real call came near me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no service funds the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my developer job and not claim a new qualification. I would not use public distress calls as private practice.

say: I want **paid call-handling practice** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **ambulance robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **dispatch decisions** using simulated calls on supervised paid time.

do: **Practise monthly simulated calls** only with both employers approving paid time and funded qualified supervision; otherwise keep coding.
**Apply for dispatcher openings** after 2031 loss only if certified paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but willing** to learn call responsibility.
S3.quote: A calm voice on a test call has to survive a real frightened caller.
fieldNote: His **training uses simulations**, two paid approvals and a funded qualified dispatcher.
Future **dispatcher work** requires completed certification, actual local paid vacancies and wages that cover household rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives emergency services time to set clear human sign-off and worker training. Robots driving ambulances and working in nurseries may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still want paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Five months saved makes our present bills secure, though a later dispatch role cannot be assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing address failures and join the staff association’s annual meeting on funded lead hours and human call sign-off. We would save 155 monthly while both wages hold and request a written retirement-income estimate; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local dispatch openings only if certified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure for the next few years. A written line of responsibility matters more than an impressive chart of call times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many funded developer hours remain and which dispatcher signs a live priority change. I would want the answer shared with staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and Salma and I will decide from our wages and verified income, not theirs.

I expect **ambulance robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I see **current bills secure** with five months saved.
do: **Keep reviewing addresses** and join annual association sign-off meeting.
**Save 155 monthly** while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Seek paid dispatch openings** after 2036 loss only if certified local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, financially secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: A written line of responsibility matters more than an impressive chart of call times.
fieldNote: His **annual group review** seeks funded lead hours and named dispatch decisions.
The **five-month cushion** supports near-term security without assuming a retirement amount, a dispatch vacancy or grown-child income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead developer wage could end before a qualified paid local emergency opening appears. Written notice, a real bill-covering vacancy and verified temporary support would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether writing dispatch software means I can answer emergency calls. A qualified dispatcher must check my practice before I take a real call.

headlineQuote: A qualified dispatcher must check my practice before I take a real call.
portrait: Victor is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, typical pay and five months saved.
He and Salma **rent** while their grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but checks dispatch tests against real service logs.
He takes **paid call training** only with employer approval, funded qualified supervision and later certification.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before a qualified paid local opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a bill-covering local vacancy and verified public support would help.
